item.title: When Your Child Wants to Know More About Their Donor
item.description:
Parenting

When Your Child Wants to Know More About Their Donor

Don't let your anxiety distract you from understanding your child.

Posted October 18, 2026

Key points
  • Feeling uncomfortable with donor conception topics is natural and belongs to you, not your child.
  • Each child will have unique ideas and feelings about their origins.
  • Learning who your child is and separating your perspective from your child's perspective is key.
Source: gpointstudio/Magnific

My "Zoom Out Theory" grew from the idea that the way we feel in the moment of decision-making can have long-term implications for our lives and the lives of our future children. One example of this is when we experience fear related to donor conception. When fear is present, it can be difficult to think calmly and separate what is happening from what we fear may happen.

Some parents experience years of infertility, loss, and grief. Others, such as those who are single parents by choice or same-sex couples, may experience fewer of these feelings but may still feel the discomfort of managing conversations with their donor-conceived child that are completely foreign to them. They worry about trying to get it "right," how the child will feel about bonding, and perhaps feel some sadness that they could not simply use their own genetics or those of their partner to build their family and instead needed to choose the genetics from someone they don’t know.

No matter how much the child is adored and wanted, these fears may loom over a parent's head, causing them to react from their own feelings rather than their child’s actual experience. They may assume the child feels the way they feel. If we zoom out, we would realize that just like adults, our children will have different temperaments. They may be the sort of person who loves to talk about their donor conception story, or perhaps they don't, or maybe, they don't think about it much at all and they are more focused on their day-to-day lives. In my practice, and on my podcast, Building Your Family, I’ve met with donor-conceived people who are interested in connecting with their donor and/or donor siblings and the sibling they grew up with is not interested in either. Part of being a parent, whether your child is donor-conceived or not, is learning who they are and supporting and loving them for exactly that. Leading with curiosity and openness so you can discover who they are is far more helpful than assumptions rooted in our own anxiety and personal experience.

To illustrate this point, here are three moments that often trigger an emotional response in parents of donor-conceived children and a different way of thinking through each one:

1. Curiosity is not rejection

Your child wanting to know more about their donor does not mean they love you any less or feel less connected to you. Children typically want to understand themselves and the world around them. For donor-conceived children, that curiosity may include questions about their genetic origins, their donor, or other people to whom they are genetically connected. These questions are about curiosity, not a reflection on how they feel about their parents. Your child can love you deeply, know beyond a shadow of a doubt that you are their parent, and be curious about where they come from. These feelings can exist together.

2. Having all the answers is less important than supporting them in their self-discovery

One of the most important things parents can communicate to their children is that it is OK to ask questions, even when the answers aren’t immediately available. You can simply say, “I don’t know, but we can find out together.” Depending on your donor arrangement, there may be questions you cannot answer and that uncertainty may make you anxious. Take comfort in knowing that your child’s experience of you being open with them, sitting with them in their uncertainty and curiosity, and being willing to discuss any subject they raise is far more important to your relationship with them and their self-esteem than any one piece of information you may or may not have about the donor. They need to know that they can continue to ask you questions as they grow and you will not shy away from them.

3. Stay where your child is

It is natural, in an anxious state, to answer the question you think your child needs to hear rather than the one that they are actually asking. For example, your child may ask if their donor has children, and rather than rushing to find out, you might tell them what you know or don’t know in that moment and then ask them if there were other things they were wondering about. Your child may respond that they wondered if they also had curly hair, if they could meet them one day, if they had three children like in your family, or maybe they want you to have another baby, or wish they could be a baby again, and that is where their mind went when they began thinking about that topic.

The more you explore, the more you will learn what they are thinking, and the answers may surprise you. It will also remind you that your child is a separate person, and not walking around the world with the same anxieties you have.

Ultimately, you want your child to feel loved for all of who they are, not just the parts that are related to you. Leading with curiosity will help them feel that you are interested in knowing them. Trust is not built in one discussion. It is built over time, one conversation at a time.

item.title: We Live in a Scary World
item.description:
Fear

We Live in a Scary World

Halloween lets us pretend we aren’t afraid for a little while.

Posted October 18, 2026

Key points
  • Halloween is an ancient holiday that focuses attention on our mortality.
  • Humans have long used traditions, fantasy, and food to cope with stress.
  • Adults can find pumpkins, costumes, and candy as comforting as children do.

In recent years, it has become popular to bemoan the commercialism of Halloween. Traditionalists argue that it used to be a child’s celebration, characterized by groups of children meandering through suburban neighborhoods to collect candy, not an opportunity for adults to dress up, attend parties, and decorate their homes and offices. But this simplistic view of the growing popularity of the holiday doesn’t reflect the facts accurately.

As befits a holiday based on mystery and drama, the history of Halloween is murky. It is believed to have started with Celtic efforts to mark the transition from summer to winter by wearing costumes and using bonfires to scare away ghosts and bad luck. Practices like carving vegetables into scary faces to repel evil spirits were brought to the U.S. by Irish immigrants in the 1800s, but by the 1920s the holiday was often marked by mean-spirited pranks. Some believe that trick-or-treating emerged out of efforts to convert the holiday to a more child-focused community event.

How Halloween Became a Modern Multi-Generational Celebration

In the 21st century, Halloween has morphed into a costume-based celebration for people of all ages characterized by parties, costume contests, and festivals. So why would a secular-based holiday, which originated centuries ago, still resonate with us? Are we simply responding to marketing efforts designed to get us to buy plastic skeletons, costumes, and candy, or are there still valid psychological reasons for our interest in this holiday? It is probably a bit of both.

Despite the fact that most of us no longer work outside, we are still diurnal creatures. We value the light, long days and abundant fresh food available in the summer. And although we can buy imported bananas any time of year, we are still attuned to seasonal changes in the colors of our yards, the leaves on our trees, and the environment around us. As the days get darker and colder, we dread the change from daylight saving time and our brains still note the shortening days. Even though electricity makes it possible for us to light our homes year-round, we still derive comfort from candles, fireplaces, and outdoor bonfires in a relatively primal way. Decorating with lights, putting candles into carved pumpkins and decorating our yards with skeletons and witches isn’t too far removed from the days when people put creepy gargoyles on buildings to scare off spirits and used bonfires to light the night. Halloween also allows us to explore our issues with mortality.

Like our ancestors, we know that we don’t live forever, so we seek ways to mark and commemorate the passage of time. From christenings to weddings to funerals, we create ceremonial events that provide us with a sense of continuity and predictability in a world over which we really don’t have a lot of control. While we no longer fear demons and witches, many of us are experiencing existential stress regarding the dangers posed by emerging threats including climate change, artificial intelligence, and global unrest. In a paradoxical way, facing our fears in a Halloween haunted house gives us the sense that we are courageous and can prevail over darker forces. Dressing as monsters, ghosts, skeletons, demons, and even celebrities, superheroes, and princesses can help us to feel that we aren’t simply victims, but can choose to play scary, powerful, or victorious characters ourselves. Doing so in the company of others provides us with a sense of belonging, which is also a significant means of stress reduction.

Costumes and Play as Stress Relief for All Ages

Dressing up in costumes, masks, and makeup can also serve as a distraction from the frustration, tedium, and stress of our daily lives. In our technologically-connected modern world, we frequently find ourselves comparing our mundane struggles to the lifestyles we see being portrayed in fabricated entertainment worlds, and carefully curated glimpses of celebrity and influencer lifestyles. Most of us are never going to walk a red carpet in an outfit that cost thousands of dollars, be a rock star, or become a supermodel. But we can still enjoy demonstrating our creativity and interests while pretending to be someone we aren’t for a day or an evening.

There is also no real reason that escaping into a temporary fantasy world should be age-limited. While children naturally spend time “playing pretend,” we all rely on our imaginations to help us understand the world and evaluate alternative choices we might make. Teens struggling to form their own identity often model their hair and clothing on people they wish to emulate, and even as adults we act, dress, and even speak differently in the company of different people. Research suggests that adult playfulness can be associated with positive health effects, reduced stress, and adaptive coping.

The Multifaceted Meaning of Halloween

It isn’t fair to talk about Halloween without mentioning candy. A recent survey indicated that 75% of Americans view Halloween as an opportunity to enjoy candy for a day without feeling guilty. Although a constant diet of candy isn’t a good idea for our health, living as we do in a culture infused with food morality and the stigmatization of weight gain means it can be freeing to give yourself permission to enjoy something that is intrinsically rewarding on an occasional basis.

As with most human endeavors, Halloween is a complicated holiday. Perhaps it doesn’t matter whether we adorn our houses with orange lights, cruise the candy aisles at our local grocery stores, create costumes for ourselves or our children, or stay home and eat popcorn and watch a horror movie. The point is that we use the holiday to think about ways to enjoy the changing seasons, the power of our imaginations, and time with the people we care about.

item.title: Free-Range Parenting Back in the News, But Not in a Good Way
item.description:
Parenting

Free-Range Parenting Back in the News, But Not in a Good Way

A conviction in Virginia reignites the debate over free-range parenting.

Posted October 18, 2026

Key points
  • Karyann Parkinson let her 5-year-old son walk by himself to a pond after they had gone together earlier.
  • Parkinson was charged and convicted of contributing to the delinquency of a minor.
  • Free-range parenting counters helicopter parenting by allowing minor setbacks as learning tools.

"Mother charged after 5-year-old walks to pond alone, stirring parenting debate." The Washington Post, September 6, 2026.

"Mom found guilty of abuse for letting 5-year-old walk outside alone speaks out." CBS News, September 7, 2026.

"I let my 5-year-old walk half a mile alone. Four days later, there was a warrant for my arrest." Business Insider, September 9, 2026.

"When Mothers Get Arrested For Mothering." The Atlantic, September 8, 2026.

"She Let Her Son Go for a Walk. Now She’s a Convicted Criminal." The Free Press, September 7, 2026.

The Incident

Source: AI-Generated

Karyann Parkinson let her 5-year-old son Samuel walk unescorted to a nearby pond to collect goose feathers. He and his mother had walked the same route earlier in the day. The Parkinson family lives in a gated community in Williamsburg, Virginia. A neighbor noticed that Samuel was walking alone and notified the security guard. He stopped Samuel, escorted him home, and called the police. Karyann Parkinson was charged and convicted of contributing to the delinquency of a minor, a Class 1 misdemeanor. She received a six-month suspended jail sentence and was put on the Virginia Child Abuse and Neglect Central Registry for seven years. Parkinson plans to appeal her conviction. This story has reignited a national debate over "free-range parenting."

Free-Range Parenting

The term "free-range parenting" was first coined by Lenore Skenazy. She is the author of Free-range kids: How parents and teachers can let go and let grow.

"By my definition, Free-Range Parenting is simply the belief that our kids are safer and smarter than our culture gives them credit for. Free-Range Parents are not hands-off. We teach our kids the old-fashioned lessons our parents taught us: Look both ways before crossing the street. Don’t go off with strangers. Let us know if you’re not going to be home when you said you’d be.

But then beyond that, we trust them to do the things on their own that many of us did at their age: walk to school, play outside, scramble eggs. We believe that giving kids some unstructured, unsupervised time when we think they’re ready isn’t crazy dangerous. It’s normal." –Lenore Skenazy

Advocates of the free-range parenting approach believe it builds resilience and self-reliance in children. Experiencing a minor negative outcome is a powerful teacher. It turns children into confident, self-sufficient adults. Free-range parenting is an antidote to helicopter over-nurturing parenting.

Helicopter Parenting

The flip-side to free-range parenting is helicopter parenting, which occurs when a parent over-nurtures their child by doing things for them that they should do themselves, making decisions for them, especially when the child is old enough to make those decisions (Clarke, Dawson, & Bredehoft, 2014). Over-nurturing involves high control, protection, and excessive involvement in a child's life. Over-nurturing can occur at any stage of a child's life. An over-nurturing parent is a so-called helicopter parent.

Research (Cui et al., 2018; Hong & Cui, 2020; Cui, 2018; Feng & Cui, 2023) shows that helicopter parenting is associated with psychological maladjustment, including symptoms of anxiety and depression, life dissatisfaction, low levels of self-control, and emotional dysregulation.

Developmental Tasks—From 3 to 6 Years of Age

According to Jean Illsley Clarke (Clarke, Dawson, & Bredehoft, 2014, p. 315-316), the following are developmental tasks that Samuel and other children his age need to accomplish. In addition, helpful parent behaviors for this stage are listed below:

Job of the child (developmental tasks)

  • To assert an identity separate from others.
  • To acquire information about the world, himself, and his body.
  • To learn that behaviors have consequences, both positive and negative.
  • To discover his effect on others and his place in groups.
  • To learn to exert power to affect relationships.
  • To learn what he has power over and what he does not have power over.
  • To do simple chores.

Helpful parent behaviors

  • Insist the child do regular, simple chores.
  • Affirm child for doing developmental tasks.
  • Continue to offer love, safety, and protection.
  • Be supportive as child continues to explore the world of things, people, ideas, and feelings.
  • Provide information about child's environment, and correct misinformation.
  • Give answers to questions.
  • Provide appropriate positive or negative consequences for actions.
  • Compliment appropriate behavior and interfere with inappropriate behavior.

The Facts in the Case

Here are the facts in Karyann Parkinson's case as reported by The Washington Post and CBS News:

  1. Both Karyann and her son Samuel had walked numerous times together to the pond where he liked to collect goose feathers.
  2. They live in a gated community in Williamsburg, Virginia.
  3. The gated community employs a full-time security guard.
  4. After they returned home from their walk on June 5, Sam asked if he could go back and look for more feathers.
  5. After about 20 to 30 minutes, there was a knock at the door. Sam was being accompanied by the security guard.
  6. A neighbor had seen him walking outside alone and called security.
  7. Security reported the incident to the local police.
  8. On June 18, police returned with a warrant for Karyann Parkinson's arrest.
  9. A Juvenile and Domestic Relations District Court judge sentenced her to six months of suspended jail time and added her name to the Virginia Abuse and Neglect Registry for seven years.
  10. Parkinson is appealing her conviction.
  11. Karyann Parkinson earned a Doctor of Law from William & Mary Law School, and a BS, in Business Family and Consumer Sciences/Human Sciences from Brigham Young University.
  12. According to both of his parents, Samuel Parkinson is a very mature, responsible now 6-year-old, and an excellent swimmer. He knows how to safely cross the street, get back home, and ask a neighbor for help if needed.

My Reaction to This Case

In this case, it appears both Samuel and his mother acted in a responsible way. Samuel is successfully working on the developmental tasks that are appropriate for his age: (1) acquiring information about the world, (2) learning that behaviors have consequences, and (3) learning what he has power over and what he does not have power over.

At the same time, his mother Karyann Parkinson demonstrated appropriate helpful parent behaviors: (1) continuing to offer love, safety, and protection, (2) being supportive as he continues to explore the world of things, people, ideas, and feelings. She insisted her son was safe and had the right to walk through the neighborhood by himself.

The judge could have read Karyann Parkinson the statute, given her a warning, and then dismissed the charges.

This still leaves an important question: "How old must a child be to do certain things without a parent accompanying them?"

item.title: Would You Harm Your Dog for Fun?
item.description:
Ethics and Morality

Would You Harm Your Dog for Fun?

How the right to trap challenges our empathy toward wildlife.

Posted October 18, 2026

Key points
  • This question speaks to the nature of human-animal relationships with companion animals and wild neighbors.
  • Human exceptionalism no longer works when we need to try to peacefully coexist with other animals.
  • Dogs’ suffering parallels that of hunted wildlife, highlighting the empathy gap in animal treatment.
Source: Neslihan Ercan/Pexels

"Colorado’s outdoors are extraordinary precisely because so many of us enjoy them in different ways. We should keep expanding outdoor recreation opportunities in a sustainable way, protecting wildlife, and finding compromises that work for everyone — not picking constitutional favorites. I urge Coloradans who hunt, fish, hike, bike or simply love our wildlife to vote “no” on Amendment 83." —Jared Polis, Governor of Colorado

Numerous people, ranging from hardcore academics to people on the streets, are keenly interested in the nature of human-animal relationships (the science of anthrozoology) including living with pets, companion animals, wild neighbors, and more distant wildlife. In my home state of Colorado, human relationships with wild neighbors and more distant wildlife are fraught with difficulty, with attitudes and values ranging from serious attempts to peacefully and compassionately coexist with these animals to equally serious attempts to harm and kill them.

What is happening in Colorado is occurring in many other states and countries, so a real-world, on-the-ground example offers a worthwhile discussion of the global complexities of our relationships with other animals.

To wit, Colorado’s Amendment 83, which will be considered by voters on Nov. 3, 2026, centers on establishing a constitutional right to hunt and trap. Trapping is on the agenda, although some people try to play it down. A web search for “Colorado amendment 83” will reveal a broad set of opinions that range from unconditional bravado and support to unconditional disgust and opposition. I'm constantly being asked what I think about 83 from Coloradans and others.

The importance of animal sentience and the emotional lives of animals

What is missing from the vast majority of opinions on this amendment, especially from those who favor it, is serious discussion of what I call the “S” and “F” words: sentience, suffering, and feelings. In other words, there is little to no consideration of the emotional lives of the nonhuman victims and what the animals themselves—those in the crosshairs—would feel about this amendment if they could have a say. Sentience simply refers to the ability to feel, and there can be no doubt that the targeted animals would vote a resounding, unanimous "no" to this amendment. There’s nothing fair about this one-sided proposal.

When you get down to it, Amendment 83 could be viewed as a constitutional right to cause cruelty—intentional physical and psychological suffering—using "traditional methods" that had been previously banned 30 years ago because they cause incredible amounts of pain and suffering, such as using steel-jaw traps, snaring, poisoning, using dogs to chase targeted animals, and baiting animals to make them easier to kill. It would also allow bears to be killed in and around their dens, including pregnant females. There's nothing fair about these abhorrent practices—just as the phrase "fair chase," when applied to so-called ethical hunting, is an obvious oxymoron.

For example, spring bear hunting was banned in Colorado in 1992—a generation ago—because it invariably resulted in killing lactating females with dependent cubs. Inarguably, these cubs need their mothers to survive. And in 1996, voters restricted the use of steel-jawed traps, snares, and poisons.

A mother bear and her cub browsing around in the Boulder Valley.
Source: Ben Owen/Pexels

The reason I chose my title for this post is because dogs are highly sentient beings, and so too are the animals who will be targeted. Dogs, wolves, cougars, black bears, beavers, and many other animals share the same feelings, ranging from joy to fear to grief and anxiety to extreme pain and suffering.

Thinking about how dogs would respond to being hunted, trapped, snared, poisoned, and subjected to other "traditional practices" brings home many of the issues surrounding the use of these cruel and injurious practices, if you will, because many people who engage in these pernicious activities also live with a canine companion. However, dogs don't suffer more than their wild relatives. Thinking about what dogs would feel can lead us to viewing them as a "gateway species" for bridging the empathy gap to include other nonhumans in the arena of compassion and peaceful coexistence and to bring humans together.

Words also matter. A good number of people who hunt and trap animals use the word "harvesting" to refer to what they are doing as if they're casually going to drink a glass of water. But this and other words, such as "cull" or "dispatch," do not sanitize these activities because animals aren't unfeeling objects to be wantonly harvested, culled, or dispatched, aka killed. If you want to harvest something, do it to corn but not to animals.

I would like to believe that if you wouldn’t include dogs in the list of victims who may be heartlessly and violently killed, you also wouldn't include other animals who also would suffer on their often slow and very painful way to dying. If you would include dogs on the menu of animals who could be hunted and trapped, many people, and I, would say we’re glad we’re not your dog.

Coda: Working for compassionate coexistence

Factoring in animal sentience is not a “radical” move but a humane and decent gesture for recognizing and appreciating who these animals truly are. And thinking about them as sentient beings is totally science-based, so if one says they follow the science, they must also factor in the science of animal emotions.

Surely we can do much better for the magnificent animals with whom we share our stunning state. The same goes for countless other places. So let's work hard for compassionate coexistence and show other animals that we deeply care about their well-being and quality of life. In fact, research shows that working for nonhumans is also good for us—a win-win for all.

item.title: Self-Compassion: Is It Wise or Wimpy?
item.description:
Wisdom

Self-Compassion: Is It Wise or Wimpy?

Practicing kindness toward yourself can fuel resilience and growth.

Posted October 18, 2026

Key points
  • Many people fear that self-compassion will make them weak or less successful.
  • Self-compassion can be tender or fierce.
  • Self-compassion can make you more capable of effectively dealing with pain and difficulties.

For decades, I lived by an unwritten rule: Keep your head down, push through, and do not feel sorry for yourself. I treated self-compassion as a risky luxury—a soft indulgence that might rob me of determination, invite self-pity, and undermine my drive. I bought into the zeitgeist that being hard on yourself was how you kept yourself accountable and succeeded in life.

Many of my clinical patients voice similar fears. One man firmly believed he didn’t deserve self-compassion if his bad choices contributed to his suffering. Yet you can offer yourself compassion and still learn from your mistakes. Punishing or berating yourself isn’t the most effective remedy. In fact, research shows that self-flagellation breeds shame and paralysis, while self-compassion creates the emotional safety required to learn, adapt, and actually change.

I understood the research intellectually, but didn't truly see the need for, and didn't practice, self-compassion until a personal tragedy rocked my world. When my son Wiley died, the sheer weight of grief thoroughly unraveled me and my previous, habituated ways of operating. It took every ounce of energy I had to navigate our new reality of life without Wiley. The self-critical, high-achieving driver in me had to take a back seat to much higher priorities.

In that dark valley, I was forced to abandon my old playbook. Self-compassion ceased to be a conceptual topic, or something only my patients needed; it became my lifeline. Treating myself with greater kindness and patience was the only way I survived the crushing weight of loss and began rebuilding a life around Wiley’s absence and a broken heart.

Two Sides of Self-Compassion

Self-compassion is the practice of meeting our pain and suffering with kindness and support. Yet psychologist Kristin Neff reminds us that self-compassion isn't just gentle comfort. It operates on two equally important, complementary axes:

  • Tender Self-Compassion (Nurturing). This is the soothing presence that meets acute pain with warmth and kindness. It may include letting yourself have a cathartic cry, taking a warm bath, resting without guilt, reaching out to a trusted friend, reading something inspirational, or being in nature or with your favorite animal. It whispers: “I see how much you’re hurting, and I’m right here with you.”
  • Fierce Self-Compassion (Protecting and Motivating). This is the proactive force that guards your boundaries and encourages wise action as a vital part of taking care of yourself. It might mean saying no, setting limits, standing up for yourself, asking for help, or having the hard conversation you’re avoiding. It asserts: “I deserve safety and respect, and I will courageously take action that protects my well-being.”

The Benefits of Self-Compassion

A substantial body of psychological research confirms that practicing self-compassion yields concrete mental health benefits:

  • It buffers against clinical anxiety, depression, rumination, and chronic stress.
  • It can reduce toxic shame, suicidal ideation, and negative thinking.
  • It fosters interpersonal empathy and healthier relationship behaviors.
  • It enhances emotional resilience, motivation, and overall life satisfaction.
  • It supports adaptive coping, self-improvement, and personal accountability.
  • It's positively associated with psychological well-being and positive states of mind.

Self-Compassion in Action

Don’t wait for a tragedy to start practicing self-compassion. The next time you encounter a setback or moment of distress, pause and try this 3-step check-in:

  • Acknowledge the Pain. Place a hand over your heart and internally state, “I feel for you in this moment of suffering.”
  • Normalize the Experience. Remind yourself, “Suffering is a natural part of being human.”
  • Ask What You Need. Inquire, “Do I need tender comfort right now, or is assertive action needed?” Then do something to help soothe yourself or improve the situation.

Self-compassion is not wimpy, and it isn't an excuse to give up. It is wise; it helps us skillfully navigate life and meet our suffering with care and support. Contrary to my initial fear that it would make me weaker, practicing self-compassion has not diminished my sense of purpose, motivation, or ability to go after my dreams and make a positive difference in the world. And it has made my interior life much kinder and more supportive.

Warmly,

Celeste Birkhofer, Ph.D.

item.title: Retirement as Personal Fulfillment: Achieving Independence
item.description:
Aging

Retirement as Personal Fulfillment: Achieving Independence

Making the transition from working to live to living your best life.

Posted October 18, 2026

Key points
  • One of the core components of a satisfying retirement is independence.
  • Retirement facilitates gaining a sense of control to promote physical and mental health.
  • Establishing new routines promotes newfound independence.
Source: Image by Pexels from Pixabay

Those who love their jobs joke that they have not “worked” a day in their lives. Yet most of us work to live, not the other way around. As we age, though, our priorities change. Older adults may decide to spend more time with loved ones and less time laboring for a paycheck. Our legacy becomes more about leaving the world a better place, not how many hours we worked. This positive attitude change impacts the way we approach retirement.

The Independence of Retirement

Researchers have studied multiple facets of retirement over the years, seeking to explore the factors that predict happiness as well as health once we exit the working world.[I] Yet some results are more relevant than others in predicting retirement satisfaction.

Anastasia Fadeeva et al. (2025) studied the factors involved in making the transition from working to retirement, focusing on positive adaptation and adjustment.[ii] Studying retired adults ages 58 to 82 who worked in both manual and non-manual occupations, they found that one of the core components was independence, navigating newfound freedom.

Fadeeva et al. describe retirement as a coveted time when former employees will shed work-associated stressors, enjoy a sense of increased control over their lives, and finally have a chance to enjoy time with loved ones. The transition can also function as a positive turning point promoting greater health and well-being through new habits. In fact, Fadeeva et al. recognize that leaving the workforce creates a window of opportunity for many retirees to create better health habits prompted by the desire to develop new goals and routines. They note this endeavor is often easier when old habits have been disrupted, as people become more receptive to new information and may acquire a fresh mindset that is open to behavior change.

Fadeeva et al. note the importance of retaining independence in retirement regarding decision-making, including decisions about new activities and roles. They note that although people value social bonds, they also value having a choice about how to socialize and with whom. This independence extends beyond freedom from social and family commitments to daily choices and leisure activities. Fadeeva et al. recognize that this reflects the desire to gain a sense of control in order to promote physical and mental health through both physical and intellectual engagement.

Independence Involves New Routines

Newfound independence and control can also come from establishing new routines. Fadeeva et al. explain that recent retirees shared that a lack of planning for new routines before or during retirement adversely impacted their sense of purpose, while people who had been retired for a while shared that having new routines enhanced their sense of satisfaction with retirement. This included new domestic arrangements, such as housekeeping responsibilities or leisure planning. In order to fully enjoy life after retirement, Fadeeva et al. suggest selecting activities based on personal preference instead of family-imposed obligations or other social duties. They share that satisfied retirees selected activities based on individual preferences, resources, and circumstances, as opposed to requirements imposed by others. Some fulfilled their desire for social interaction through selecting certain groups or exercise clubs, while others made choices based on health benefits or geographically specific opportunities. The key to retirement satisfaction involves accommodating individual differences to accommodate autonomy.

The Autonomy of Independence

A common denominator among satisfied, happy, healthy, well-adjusted retirees is enjoyment of their independence, sometimes for the first time. This doesn’t necessarily mean spending time alone; it means having the choice about how to spend time. Retirement affords the chance to spend time with loved ones, practice one’s faith, pursue philanthropic passions, or finally crack open the book that has been sitting on the nightstand for years. So, work hard, retire responsibly, and pursue integrity through independence.
